slides.title: The problem and seven classes
slides.notes: An image receives one of seven appearance labels. This could help search a rendered asset library. The categories are wood, metal, stone, concrete, ceramic, fabric and leather. Each picture is an actual held-out render selected by path, without filtering by correctness. The same sphere makes texture and reflectance informative, but this does not identify physical composition. In the development collection, ceramic includes mosaic or terrazzo-like appearances and concrete includes plaster or painted walls.

items.text: Classify material appearance to support browsing of rendered assets
Appearance categories do not establish physical composition.

slides.title: Dataset provenance and group separation
slides.notes: The study has 3,780 balanced RGB images at 512 by 512 pixels, with 30 rendered views per material. Development contains 450 images per class and the fresh holdout 90 per class. Source textures come from Poly Haven and ambientCG under CC0. They include scanned and procedural assets, so we do not describe all sources as independent physical scans. Labels follow audited asset identity and appearance. Known generator relatives are merged into groups. Thirty views of a texture remain correlated. No known development-to-holdout family or exact-map reuse remains, but unknown physical ancestry cannot be ruled out. The rendered-dataset release licence is still an owner decision.

items.text: 30 views per material. Each class has 450 development + 90 test images.

slides.title: Three model families, four pipelines
slides.notes: ConvNeXt is a modern convolutional model, ResNet is a residual convolutional network, and DINOv2 uses a vision transformer. All use pretrained weights. A frozen ConvNeXt control and fixed ResNet baseline provide family comparisons. The primary fuses DINOv2 and ConvNeXt features and fits a scaled, class-balanced logistic classifier. DINO pools CLS, patch mean and patch standard deviation at two resolutions, excluding register tokens from patch pooling. The partially fine-tuned DINO model is exploratory. These are complete pipeline comparisons because pretraining data, resolution and compute budgets differ.

slides.title: Experimental setup
slides.notes: The frozen selection uses five outer source-group folds and three inner grouped folds, seed 20261027. Inner folds select five representations and C in 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 by Macro F1. The scaler and classifier are fitted inside each training partition. All original images are development data because the historical test had already been consulted. The neural comparison uses the same development pool and the same final holdout. DINO searches two learning rates in a bounded three-fold exploratory follow-up. Preprocessing converts to RGB, uses model-specific resize and centre crop and pretrained normalisation. Neural training alone adds small random crops, horizontal flips and mild colour jitter. ResNet uses AdamW with a cosine schedule for ten fixed epochs. DINO uses AdamW and development early stopping, then a fixed five-epoch final fit. Both have effective batch size 32, label-smoothed cross entropy and weight decay 0.01. Development Macro F1 selected the frozen primary before any fresh scores. Four fixed models then received one clean evaluation each.

slides.title: Actual learning curves
slides.notes: These are the complete recorded histories for all three development folds at the selected DINO backbone learning rate of 1e-5. Solid curves show training and dashed curves development validation. No curve is a fresh-test result. The training fit becomes strong while validation varies by source fold. Validation chooses the learning rate and epoch count, so it is optimistic for that selection. The six-fit search also includes 3e-6, whose mean best development Macro F1 was 0.76250 versus 0.77248 at 1e-5. Best epochs 6, 5 and 3 imply five final epochs. ResNet has actual training-only logs for its fixed schedule and no epoch-wise validation curve. The frozen logistic head has regularisation-search diagnostics, not neural learning epochs.

items.text: DINOv2, selected learning rate 1e-5. Solid: training. Dashed: development validation.
Training fit improves faster than validation. Fresh test data never set epochs.

slides.title: Clean test results on unseen sources
slides.notes: The primary achieves 505 correct images out of 630, or 80.16%, with Macro F1 0.7952. Its 95% source-group bootstrap interval is 66.03 to 93.65%. The point target of 80% is met but the lower bound is below 80%. Fine-tuned DINOv2 records 86.83% and Macro F1 0.8631. It stays an exploratory comparison. Its paired accuracy advantage over the primary is 6.67 percentage points with interval minus 2.06 to plus 16.19, which includes zero. Thus the ranking does not establish superiority. The control interval is 61.59 to 88.73%, ResNet 63.65 to 90.48%, and DINOv2 76.98 to 95.87%. Intervals use 10,000 class-stratified cluster draws over 21 sources, conditional on these saved predictions.

items.text: The 80% point target is met. The lower confidence bound is below 80%.

Exploratory DINOv2 advantage: +6.67 pp, paired 95% CI -2.06 to +16.19 pp.

slides.title: Primary errors and per-class performance
slides.notes: Read the matrix by rows: true class first, prediction second. Every row has 90 images. Ceramic is often called stone, with 30 of its 90 images following that error. Leather is called concrete in 22 cases. Wood, metal and fabric reach perfect recall on the three sampled sources per class, which is not a population guarantee. Ceramic precision is 1.000 but recall is only 0.578, illustrating that missing many examples can coexist with few false positive labels. All values are saved point metrics, not newly scored results.

slides.notes: These four examples use the saved primary predictions. The correct wood and metal examples are from the unfiltered class gallery. The ceramic and leather failures come from the report error gallery. They are selected illustrations rather than a representative performance estimate. Point to visual ambiguity in texture and reflectance as a plausible explanation, not a causal attribution. Model probabilities can be high for wrong answers and are not calibrated certainty. slides.title: JPEG compression exposes a weakness
slides.notes: These saved corruption results use the same 630 images and five deterministic transforms. The primary drops from 80.16% clean accuracy to 59.05% at JPEG quality 30, a 21.11 percentage point loss. DINOv2 falls from 86.83% to 75.40%. Primary corruption tests were predeclared, whereas the DINOv2 corruption comparison was applied after observing clean and primary-corruption scores and is explicitly post hoc. Compression is the largest degradation here, but these tests do not substitute for new scenes or real-camera data.

items.text: Primary: 80.16% clean to 59.05% at JPEG quality 30
DINOv2 corruption results are a post hoc exploratory comparison.

slides.title: Efficiency and model recommendation
slides.notes: On the recorded RTX 4070 Laptop GPU, ResNet has the lowest warm batch-one median latency. The primary is slower because it uses multiple backbone passes. Required storage includes the backbones, not just the small classifier head. Timing starts from predecoded RGB and includes preprocessing and probabilities, but excludes disk reading and decoding. These are CUDA measurements, not classroom CPU measurements. Keep frozen fusion as the preselected study result. Fine-tuned DINOv2 is a promising next deployment candidate because it has higher observed accuracy and lower measured latency than the primary, but it needs an independently planned confirmation. Choose ResNet only if the speed trade-off is acceptable.

slides.title: Limitations and next experiment
slides.notes: Only 21 new groups, three per class, give wide uncertainty despite 630 images. Asset provenance is audited but some common physical ancestry and backbone pretraining overlap may remain unknown. Sources combine scanned and procedural textures, and restricted class definitions and renderer differences affect transfer. No genuine photograph test has been performed. Pipeline comparison also combines architecture, resolution, pretraining and compute changes. The next experiment should be frozen before data collection, add more independent sources in ceramic, concrete, stone and leather, vary scene and camera, include real photographs, and test compression systematically. Reusing this now-scored holdout for tuning would require another fresh assessment.

slides.title: Material Studio demo and conclusion
slides.notes: Use the separate classroom guide. The expected app sequence is Classify, Results, then Dataset. Select an image or built-in sample and model, start a prediction, let the loading state complete, and inspect probabilities. Only call this a live prediction after the actual runtime has completed inference for that input. In Results, compare stored model metrics and confusions, then inspect the class gallery in Dataset. The app is under parallel integration and this workflow is not yet verified here. If runtime inference is unavailable, explicitly announce the offline fallback and use stored results or slide 9 examples. Conclude that source-aware evaluation supports the primary point target, but uncertainty and compression weakness limit broad claims.
